rv.q: The production is full of pace and creepiness when it could so easily slide into the ridiculous.
Folk horror with an urban twist

The novel’s reputation rests not on plot, character or even theme, but on voice. It is a book composed of fragments, whispers and interruptions, a work that dissolves the boundary between the people of a village and the place itself.

Adapted for the stage by award-winning West Country playwright Bea Roberts and directed by Nancy Medina , Lanny is a dark and powerful blend of reality, folklore and imagination. It’s a story of belonging, curiosity for the unknown, and facing fears.

It’s never consistently scary enough (though the few moments where the play truly leans into terror are shocking and tremendous), nor really funny enough, with most of the jokes landing with a thud, feeling like duds cut out of Jez Butterworth’s Jerusalem .
